intro: Louisiana’s graduated brackets make the state deduction change as taxable pay rises rather than staying at one fixed percentage. This Louisiana paycheck calculator follows the R-1210 2026 formula and reflects state withholding elections made through Form L-4.
taxSummary: Louisiana uses graduated income-tax brackets from 1.85% to 4.25%, with withholding administered by the Louisiana Department of Revenue. Employees use Form L-4 for Louisiana withholding elections, while payroll applies the state’s withholding rules to each check. The calculator uses the "Louisiana R-1210 2026 formula." Because the system is graduated, the effective Louisiana withholding percentage can change with earnings and filing circumstances instead of matching one statewide rate on every paycheck.

sections.h3: How Louisiana Form L-4 feeds the state withholding calculation
sections.p: Form L-4 supplies Louisiana-specific withholding elections for your employer’s payroll calculation. Those elections are applied through the state withholding method rather than by taking one percentage directly from gross wages. Louisiana’s graduated brackets run from 1.85% to 4.25%, so the resulting state deduction can change as the wages presented to the calculation change. The calculator uses the Louisiana R-1210 2026 formula for this process. If you update your L-4 information, calculate the Louisiana line again instead of carrying forward an effective percentage from an earlier paycheck. The state form affects Louisiana withholding specifically, while other payroll deductions continue to follow their own calculations.

sections.h3: Louisiana’s single examples show the graduated pattern
sections.p: At $45,000 single, biweekly gross pay is $1,730.77 and Louisiana state income tax is $38.18. The effective state rate is 2.21%, and the resulting paycheck is $1,436.34 after the listed deductions. Increase the salary to $65,000 and gross biweekly pay becomes $2,500.00. Louisiana withholding rises to $61.95, while the effective state rate increases to 2.48% and net pay becomes $2,030.65. The state deduction therefore grows by more than simply preserving the first example’s effective percentage. Louisiana’s graduated structure and R-1210 formula recalculate withholding as earnings change, which is why scaling a previous state deduction is not a reliable shortcut.

sections.h3: What pre-tax deductions can change in a Louisiana calculation
sections.p: Louisiana withholding is based on wages processed through the state formula, so payroll items that alter the wages subject to state withholding can also alter the Louisiana line. The $45,000, $65,000, $90,000, and $130,000 examples contain no 401(k) contribution or pre-tax benefits, allowing the income levels to be compared without those additional variables. If your own paycheck contains qualifying pre-tax deductions, include their treatment when modeling Louisiana withholding instead of subtracting every benefit only after taxes have been calculated. This matters in a graduated system because changing taxable wages can change not just the dollar amount withheld but also the effective state withholding percentage produced by the calculation.

sections.h3: Louisiana hourly wages still run through the R-1210 formula
sections.p: Hourly workers use the same Louisiana withholding framework, but the wages entering the calculation can move from one paycheck to the next. Start by determining the period’s earnings with the hourly paycheck calculator, then apply your Louisiana withholding information. The salary examples use biweekly payroll across 26 pay periods, creating fixed gross amounts such as $2,500.00 at $65,000. A changing work schedule can instead produce different taxable wages each payday. Because Louisiana uses graduated brackets, a larger or smaller paycheck does not have to preserve the same effective state withholding percentage. Recalculating the Louisiana line for the actual pay period is more useful than multiplying a previous deduction by the change in hours.

sections.h3: Louisiana filing status changes the relationship between income and withholding
sections.p: The married filing jointly examples illustrate why annual salary alone does not determine Louisiana’s effective withholding rate. At $90,000, Louisiana state income tax is $76.36 per biweekly paycheck and the effective state rate is 2.21%. At $130,000, the state deduction rises to $123.90 and the effective rate becomes 2.48%. Those effective rates match the corresponding single examples at different income levels rather than increasing strictly with salary across all four cases. Filing circumstances therefore matter alongside earnings when the R-1210 formula is applied. When your household filing setup changes, calculate the Louisiana withholding under the appropriate configuration instead of assuming the state deduction should track salary by a fixed percentage.

faqs.q: What is Louisiana Form L-4 used for?
faqs.a: Form L-4 provides Louisiana-specific withholding elections used in the state payroll calculation. The calculator applies those elections through the Louisiana R-1210 2026 formula rather than treating the state deduction as one fixed percentage of gross wages.

faqs.q: Why does my Louisiana withholding percentage change with income?
faqs.a: Louisiana uses graduated income-tax brackets from 1.85% to 4.25%. At $45,000 single, the example shows $38.18 of Louisiana withholding and a 2.21% effective state rate; at $65,000 single, those figures become $61.95 and 2.48%.

faqs.q: What is the Louisiana paycheck result at $90,000 married filing jointly?
faqs.a: At $90,000 married filing jointly, biweekly gross pay is $3,461.54. Louisiana state income tax is $76.36, and after $247.69 of federal income tax, $214.62 of Social Security, and $50.19 of Medicare, the paycheck is $2,872.68.

faqs.q: Which Louisiana withholding method applies in the calculator?
faqs.a: The calculator uses the Louisiana R-1210 2026 formula. That method applies Louisiana’s withholding rules to payroll wages and state elections, allowing the state deduction to respond to income and filing circumstances within the graduated tax structure.

intro: Maryland payroll has a strong location component because county income tax sits alongside the graduated state tax. This Maryland paycheck calculator separates the 2026 state schedule from an entered county planning rate so you can model both layers.
taxSummary: Maryland combines graduated state income tax with county-level income tax, and the Comptroller of Maryland administers the state system. Your county of residence can materially affect the total amount withheld from wages. The calculator uses the "Maryland 2026 state schedule + entered county planning rate," keeping the county component distinct from the state schedule. The four salary examples contain no local tax, so their Maryland withholding figures provide a state-only starting point before an applicable county planning rate is entered.

sections.h3: Why your Maryland county belongs in the paycheck calculation
sections.p: County income tax is a central part of Maryland payroll rather than a minor detail that can be ignored when estimating take-home pay. The applicable county amount varies by county of residence, so two Maryland employees with identical salaries can have different total withholding when they live in different counties. The calculator handles this through an entered county planning rate alongside the Maryland state schedule. Its reference salary examples leave local tax empty, which isolates the statewide calculation. To model your own paycheck, treat the county component as a separate input instead of increasing the state rate or assuming the state deduction already contains every Maryland income-tax amount that may apply.

sections.h3: A $65,000 Maryland paycheck before county tax is entered
sections.p: At $65,000 single, biweekly gross pay is $2,500.00. Federal income tax is $216.15, Social Security is $155.00, and Medicare is $36.25. Maryland state income tax is $112.54 under the state schedule, leaving $1,980.06 per paycheck and $51,481.50/year. The effective state rate shown is 4.50%. Because this example has no local tax entered, it does not yet reflect an applicable county planning rate. At $45,000 single, Maryland state income tax is $76.00 and net pay is $1,398.52. Adding the relevant county component would reduce the paycheck beyond these state-only examples.

sections.h3: Maryland residency can matter when your job is across a county line
sections.p: Maryland’s county income-tax structure makes residence especially relevant for workers who commute between counties. Your employer’s worksite and your home county are not interchangeable details when the county tax is tied to residence. If you change where you live while keeping the same job and salary, the county portion of your payroll calculation can change even though the Maryland state schedule does not. That makes county information worth reviewing whenever you move within Maryland. The calculator’s separate county planning-rate input is designed for this local layer, allowing you to leave the state calculation intact while changing the location-sensitive component of the estimate.

sections.h3: How Maryland’s state deduction changes across married examples
sections.p: At $90,000 married filing jointly, the calculator produces $158.21 of Maryland state income tax from $3,461.54 of biweekly gross pay. The effective state rate is 4.57%, and the paycheck is $2,790.83 before any local tax is entered. At $130,000 married filing jointly, gross pay rises to $5,000.00, Maryland state income tax becomes $231.29, and the effective state rate reaches 4.63%. Net pay is $3,953.90 under the same no-local-tax setup. The progression reflects Maryland’s graduated state schedule. County income tax is an additional layer, so these figures should not be interpreted as the complete Maryland income-tax burden for every resident.

sections.h3: Maryland hourly workers need both wages and county information
sections.p: For hourly work, calculate the wages earned during the pay period with the hourly paycheck calculator before applying Maryland’s state schedule. Then include the county planning rate that corresponds to your residence when a county tax applies. This matters because variable hours can change the wages entering the graduated state calculation while a move between counties can change the local component independently. The salary examples use 26 biweekly pay periods, so they do not have that paycheck-to-paycheck wage variation. Maryland workers with changing schedules should therefore model the actual period rather than converting one example’s state deduction into an assumed fixed percentage.

faqs.q: Why does my Maryland county affect paycheck withholding?
faqs.a: Maryland adds county-level income tax to its graduated state income tax, and the county component varies by county of residence. The calculator keeps that local amount separate through an entered county planning rate, so location can change total withholding even when salary stays the same.

faqs.q: Is Maryland county tax included in the $65,000 example?
faqs.a: No local tax is entered in that example. At $65,000 single, the calculator shows $112.54 of Maryland state income tax and $1,980.06 of net biweekly pay. An applicable county planning rate would add another Maryland-related deduction.

faqs.q: Can moving to another Maryland county change my paycheck?
faqs.a: Yes, because Maryland county income tax varies by county of residence. A move can therefore change the county portion of withholding even when your employer, salary, and the statewide Maryland tax calculation remain unchanged.

faqs.q: Why does Maryland withholding rise between the $90,000 and $130,000 examples?
faqs.a: Maryland uses a graduated state income-tax schedule. The married filing jointly examples show state withholding increasing from $158.21 at $90,000 to $231.29 at $130,000. Those figures exclude an entered county tax, which is calculated as a separate local component.

sections.h3: Massachusetts keeps a consistent effective state rate in these examples

sections.h3: Breaking down Massachusetts pay at $90,000 married filing jointly

sections.h3: Where the Massachusetts high-earner surtax fits into the tax structure
sections.p: Massachusetts generally has a 5% income-tax rate, but the state structure also includes an additional 4% surtax applying to income above $1 million. None of the four salary examples reaches that income level: they cover $45,000, $65,000, $90,000, and $130,000. As a result, these examples are useful for understanding the ordinary wage-tax and payroll-premium pattern but do not illustrate the high-earner surtax in action. If your income reaches the surtax range, do not extrapolate from the effective state rates shown in these four examples. The additional Massachusetts tax mechanism becomes relevant beyond the income levels represented here.

sections.h3: How employer-plan deductions can affect Massachusetts taxable wages
sections.p: The reference paychecks contain no 401(k) contribution and no pre-tax benefits. If your employer-plan deductions change wages used for Massachusetts income-tax withholding, the state income-tax line can differ from the salary examples even before considering the PFML component. Keep the two effects conceptually separate: one concerns the wages entering the income-tax calculation, while the other is the state payroll premium represented through the entered PFML employee share. This distinction is useful in Massachusetts because both can affect the final deposit while appearing for different reasons. Enter payroll benefits according to their treatment rather than subtracting every employer-plan deduction only after the state calculation.

faqs.q: Why does my Massachusetts paycheck show PFML separately?

faqs.q: What Massachusetts deductions appear at $90,000 married filing jointly?

faqs.q: When does the Massachusetts high-earner surtax matter?

faqs.q: Why is the effective state rate 5.08% in all four Massachusetts examples?
